Credit Score Dataset — EDA & Data Quality Assessment

Dataset: CreditScore.csv (150,000 borrowers × 13 variables) · Target: SeriousDlqin2yrs (1 = 90+ days past due / worse within 2 years)

Workflow: (1) Data understanding & quality report → (2) EDA → (3) Cleaning & preparation → (4) Final findings.

Every important chart is followed by a short Key insight, and every cleaning decision is justified.

What this already tells us

  • Only three columns contain missing values: Gender (≈99.8 %), MonthlyIncome (≈19.8 %) and NumberOfDependents (≈2.6 %).
  • The numeric ranges are suspicious: Age min = 0, RevolvingUtilization max ≈ 50,708 (a ratio that should be ~0–1), DebtRatio max ≈ 329,664, MonthlyIncome max ≈ 3 million, and all three past-due counters have a max of 98 while their 75th percentile is 0.
  • NumberOfDependents is stored as float only because it contains NaN; Gender is a text column that is almost empty.

1.2 Missing values — how much, and is it random?

miss = raw.isna().sum(); miss = miss[miss>0]
print(miss.to_frame('missing').assign(pct=lambda d: (d.missing/len(raw)*100).round(2)))

Interpretation

  • Gender is essentially unusable: only 307 of 150,000 rows (0.2 %) have a value, and they all sit in the first ≈16k Ids — i.e. it was captured for one slice of the data only (not random). It can neither be imputed credibly nor used as a feature (and using gender in credit decisions is regulated/ethically sensitive anyway).
  • MonthlyIncome is missing for ~20 % of borrowers; every row with missing NumberOfDependents is also missing income, so both gaps come from the same source (probably borrowers whose profile wasn’t fully captured). The default rate differs between missing/present income (5.6 % vs 6.9 %), so the missingness itself is informative → we will keep an indicator flag.

Interpretation: There are no exact duplicate records (every Id is unique). Ignoring Id, 608 rows repeat another row's feature values. Inspecting them shows they are mostly “thin-file / inactive” profiles (91 % have no late payments at all and their default rate is only 3.3 %, half the average) — exactly the profiles where different real people will share identical values. Since the Ids are distinct and nothing shows a repeated-ingestion pattern, they are not true duplicates and will be kept (dropping them would bias the data against low-activity borrowers).

Largest "real" value in the counters: {'NumberOfTime30-59DaysPastDueNotWorse': 13, 'NumberOfTime60-89DaysPastDueNotWorse': 11, 'NumberOfTimes90DaysLate': 17}

Interpretation

  • One borrower has Age = 0 — impossible for a credit applicant (the next-smallest age is 21) → a data-entry error. 13 borrowers are older than 100 (max 109); this is rare but possible/unverifiable, so they are kept.
  • The values 96 and 98 appear in 269 rows, always simultaneously in all three past-due columns — a person can’t be 98 times late in each bucket while the real maximum is 17. These are special codes (typically “unknown / not applicable”), not counts. They are also far from random: 54.6 % of these rows defaulted vs ~6 % otherwise, so they must be handled carefully rather than just deleted.

Of all rows with DebtRatio > 1, share whose income is missing or 0: 0.837
Of rows with DebtRatio > 10, share whose income is missing or 0: 0.977

Interpretation — the most important discovery in the data

  • DebtRatio should be debt ÷ income, i.e. a number mostly between 0 and 1. For borrowers with valid income its median is ≈0.29 (99th percentile ≈ 3). But for borrowers whose income is missing or 0, the median “ratio” is ≈900–1,150 – clearly a dollar amount of debt, not a ratio (dividing by a missing/zero income is impossible, so the raw debt figure was stored instead).
  • ~23 % of rows have DebtRatio > 1, and ≈84 % of them (≈98 % of those > 10) have missing/zero income. So the huge values are not random outliers; they are a systematic data-definition problem tied to income.
  • Utilisation > 1 is possible (over the credit limit), but values above 2 (hundreds of rows, up to 50,708) are implausible; the 99.9th percentile is ≈1,571.
  • MonthlyIncome = 0 (1,634 rows) has the same “dollar-style” DebtRatio, which suggests a zero here means unknown rather than genuinely no income.

1.5 📋 Data Quality Report (summary)

#IssueEvidenceSeverityPlanned action
1Gender almost empty & non-random99.8 % missing; non-null only in Ids ≤ ~16kHighStandardise m/f→Male/Female, then drop from modelling
2Special codes 96/98 in past-due counters269 rows, all three columns at once, 54.6 % defaultHighReplace by NaN, add flag LateCodeFlag, impute 0 (median)
3DebtRatio is not a ratio when income is missing/0median ≈1,000 vs 0.29; 84 % of DebtRatio>1 rowsHighTreat as unreliable → flag IncomeUnknown, impute DebtRatio
4MonthlyIncome missing (19.8 %) + zeros (1,634)informative missingnessMediumMedian imputation by age band + IncomeUnknown flag
5Impossible/extreme valuesAge = 0 (1 row); utilisation up to 50,708; income up to 3.0 MMediumRemove age-0 row; cap utilisation, income, DebtRatio, counts
6NumberOfDependents missing (2.6 %), wrong dtypeall inside the income-missing groupLowImpute 0 (mode), convert to integer
7608 feature-duplicates (ignoring Id)thin-file profiles, distinct IdsLowInvestigated → keep
8Class imbalanceonly 6.68 % positivesInfoHandle at modelling stage

2. Exploratory Data Analysis

For EDA the sentinel codes (96/98) are masked as NaN in the past-due columns, otherwise they would distort every plot; heavily skewed variables are shown on clipped or log scales (the clipping is for display only — the actual cleaning is done in Section 3).

eda = raw.copy()
eda['LateSentinel'] = (eda[LATE]>=96).any(axis=1)
eda[LATE] = eda[LATE].where(eda[LATE]<96)           # mask 96/98 for plotting only
eda['Gender'] = eda.Gender.str.lower().map({'m':'Male','f':'Female'})
eda['LogIncome'] = np.log1p(eda.MonthlyIncome)
eda['Util_clip'] = eda.RevolvingUtilizationOfUnsecuredLines.clip(upper=2)
eda['DebtRatio_clip'] = eda.DebtRatio.clip(upper=3)
print('EDA copy ready:', eda.shape)
EDA copy ready: (150000, 17)

2.1 Target variable

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11,4))
cnt = eda[TARGET].value_counts().sort_index()
sns.countplot(data=eda, x=TARGET, ax=ax[0], palette=['#4C72B0','#C44E52'])
for p in ax[0].patches: ax[0].annotate(f'{int(p.get_height()):,}\n({p.get_height()/len(eda)*100:.2f}%)', (p.get_x()+p.get_width()/2, p.get_height()), ha='center', va='bottom')
ax[0].set_title('Distribution of SeriousDlqin2yrs'); ax[0].set_ylim(0, cnt.max()*1.15)
ax[1].pie(cnt, labels=['0 – no delinquency','1 – delinquency'], autopct='%1.2f%%', colors=['#4C72B0','#C44E52'], startangle=90, explode=(0,.08))
ax[1].set_title('Class share'); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print('Imbalance ratio  majority:minority = %.1f : 1' % (cnt[0]/cnt[1]))
Imbalance ratio  majority:minority = 14.0 : 1

Key insight: The target is strongly imbalanced – only 6.68 % (10,026) of borrowers defaulted vs 93.32 % who did not (≈14 : 1). A model that always predicts “no delinquency” would be 93 % accurate, so accuracy is a misleading metric and stratified splits, class weights/resampling and metrics such as AUC / PR-AUC / recall will be needed.

2.2 Univariate analysis — numerical variables (histogram + KDE)

num_plots = [('Age','Age (years)'), ('LogIncome','log(1 + MonthlyIncome)'), ('Util_clip','Revolving utilisation (clipped at 2)'),

Key insights:

  • Age is roughly bell-shaped (mean ≈ 52, concentrated 40–65), while income is extremely right-skewed (skew ≈ 114; utilisation and DebtRatio ≈ 95–98) and only looks normal after a log transform — typical of monetary variables.
  • Utilisation is bimodal: a big spike near 0 (people not using their credit) and another near 1 (maxed-out lines). DebtRatio is piled at 0–1 with a long tail; the skewness of the raw variables (≈ 95–114 for income, utilisation and DebtRatio) confirms we must treat outliers before modelling.

2.3 Univariate analysis — categorical / count variables (count plots)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(16,8))
sns.countplot(data=eda.dropna(subset=['Gender']), x='Gender', ax=axes[0,0], palette='deep'); axes[0,0].set_title(f'Gender (only {eda.Gender.notna().sum()} non-null rows)')
sns.countplot(x=eda.NumberOfDependents.dropna().clip(upper=6).astype(int), ax=axes[0,1], color='#4C72B0'); axes[0,1].set_title('Number of dependents (6 = 6+)'); axes[0,1].set_xlabel('')
sns.countplot(x=eda.NumberRealEstateLoansOrLines.clip(upper=6), ax=axes[0,2], color='#4C72B0'); axes[0,2].set_title('Real-estate loans (6 = 6+)'); axes[0,2].set_xlabel('')
for ax,c in zip(axes[1], LATE):
    sns.countplot(x=eda[c].dropna().clip(upper=6).astype(int), ax=ax, color='#DD8452'); ax.set_title(c.replace('NumberOf','') + ' (6 = 6+)', fontsize=10); ax.set_xlabel(''); ax.set_yscale('log')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Key insights:

  • Gender: 223 males vs 84 females out of 150,000 rows – too small and non-random to say anything about the population.
  • The past-due counters (log-scale on the bottom row) are dominated by 0: ~84–95 % of borrowers have never been late in a given bucket, so these are highly zero-inflated count variables. ≈59 % of borrowers have no dependents; most have 0–2.

2.4 Outlier view — boxplots

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(18,8))
vars_raw = ['Age','MonthlyIncome','RevolvingUtilizationOfUnsecuredLines','DebtRatio']
for ax,c in zip(axes[0], vars_raw):
    sns.boxplot(y=eda[c], ax=ax, color='#8FB1D8'); ax.set_title(f'{c} (raw)', fontsize=10)
    if c!='Age': ax.set_yscale('symlog')
vars_by = [('Age','Age'),('LogIncome','log income'),('Util_clip','Utilisation (clip 2)'),('DebtRatio_clip','DebtRatio (clip 3)')]
for ax,(c,t) in zip(axes[1], vars_by):
    sns.boxplot(data=eda, x=TARGET, y=c, ax=ax, palette=['#4C72B0','#C44E52']); ax.set_title(f'{t} by target', fontsize=10); ax.set_xlabel('SeriousDlqin2yrs')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Key insights: On the raw scale (top row, symlog axis) income, utilisation and DebtRatio contain points orders of magnitude above the box – extreme outliers that need capping. By target (bottom row), defaulters are younger and have higher utilisation with a lower median log-income, while DebtRatio looks nearly identical for both groups – an early hint that raw DebtRatio is a weak/noisy predictor.

Key insight: Delinquency falls steadily with age: ≈11 % for borrowers under 36 vs ≈2–3 % for those over 65 (mean age 45.9 for defaulters vs 52.8 for non-defaulters). Age is a strong, monotonic, easily-explained risk driver.

MonthlyIncome vs target

d['IncomeDecile'] = pd.qcut(d.MonthlyIncome, 10, duplicates='drop')

sns.barplot(x=mi.index, y=mi.values, ax=ax[2], color='#DD8452'); ax[2].set_title('Default rate (%): income missing vs present')
for i,v in enumerate(mi.values): ax[2].text(i, v+.05, f'{v:.2f}', ha='center')

Key insight: Higher income means lower risk – default rate drops from ≈8.4–9.7 % in the bottom deciles to ≈4.5 % in the top two (median income 4,500 for defaulters vs 5,466 for non-defaulters). The relationship is non-linear/flattening and the mean is dominated by outliers, so the median / log scale is the right summary; missing income carries a different default rate (5.6 %), supporting a missing-indicator flag.

DebtRatio vs target

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(17,4.5))
b=[-.001,.25,.5,1,2,10,1e7]; l=['0-0.25','0.25-0.5','0.5-1','1-2','2-10','>10']
eda['DebtBand']=pd.cut(eda.DebtRatio,bins=b,labels=l)
dr = eda.groupby('DebtBand')[TARGET].mean()*100
sns.barplot(x=dr.index.astype(str), y=dr.values, ax=ax[0], color='#C44E52'); ax[0].set_title('Default rate (%) by DebtRatio band'); ax[0].set_xlabel('DebtRatio')
for i,v in enumerate(dr.values): ax[0].text(i, v+.1, f'{v:.1f}', ha='center')
shr = eda.groupby('DebtBand').MonthlyIncome.apply(lambda s: s.isna().mean()*100)
sns.barplot(x=shr.index.astype(str), y=shr.values, ax=ax[1], color='#8C8C8C'); ax[1].set_title('% of rows with MISSING income, by DebtRatio band'); ax[1].set_xlabel('DebtRatio')
ok = eda[(eda.MonthlyIncome>0)]
dr2 = ok.groupby(pd.cut(ok.DebtRatio,[-.001,.25,.5,1,2,1e7],labels=['0-0.25','0.25-0.5','0.5-1','1-2','>2']))[TARGET].mean()*100
sns.barplot(x=dr2.index.astype(str), y=dr2.values, ax=ax[2], color='#4C72B0'); ax[2].set_title('Default rate (%) – only rows with income > 0'); ax[2].set_xlabel('DebtRatio')
for i,v in enumerate(dr2.values): ax[2].text(i, v+.1, f'{v:.1f}', ha='center')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Key insight: On the raw data DebtRatio has no sensible pattern – the default rate falls again for ratios above 2 and the “>10” band is 93 % missing-income rows (middle chart), confirming those values are dollar amounts, not ratios. Restricting to borrowers with valid income (right chart) restores a clear rising pattern (the >2 group, 1,786 rows, falls back to 7.6 %, so it is probably still noisy): risk rises from ≈6 % at low ratios to ≈14 % at ratios 1–2 (the few >2 values are noisy), so DebtRatio is only informative after the income issue is handled.

Utilisation, delinquency history and dependents vs target

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(17,4.5))
ub=[-.001,.25,.5,.75,1,2,1e7]; ul=['0-.25','.25-.5','.5-.75','.75-1','1-2','>2']
u = eda.groupby(pd.cut(eda.RevolvingUtilizationOfUnsecuredLines,ub,labels=ul))[TARGET].mean()*100
sns.barplot(x=u.index.astype(str), y=u.values, ax=axes[0], color='#C44E52'); axes[0].set_title('Default rate (%) by credit utilisation')
for i,v in enumerate(u.values): axes[0].text(i, v+.5, f'{v:.1f}', ha='center')
for c,col in zip(LATE, ['#4C72B0','#DD8452','#55A868']):
    s = eda[c].clip(upper=6); axes[1].plot(sorted(s.dropna().unique()), (eda.groupby(s)[TARGET].mean()*100).values, marker='o', label=c.replace('NumberOfTime','').replace('NumberOfTimes','').replace('PastDueNotWorse',''), color=col)
axes[1].set_title('Default rate (%) by # of past-due events (6 = 6+)'); axes[1].legend(fontsize=8); axes[1].set_xlabel('count')
dp = eda.groupby(eda.NumberOfDependents.clip(upper=5))[TARGET].mean()*100
sns.barplot(x=dp.index.astype(int), y=dp.values, ax=axes[2], color='#8FB1D8'); axes[2].set_title('Default rate (%) by dependents (5 = 5+)')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Key insights:

  • Utilisation is a very strong driver: default rate climbs from ≈2 % (below 25 % utilisation) to ≈18 % (75–100 %) and ≈40 % for 1–2× the limit. (The >2 band drops to ≈15 %, another sign that those huge values are unreliable.)
  • Past-due history is the strongest signal of all: one prior 90-day delinquency lifts default from ≈4.6 % to ≈34 %, and 3+ events to ≈58–67 %. Even a single 30-59-day lateness takes the rate from 4 % to 15 %. Dependents have only a mild effect (≈6 % at 0 → ≈10 % at 4+).

2.6 Correlation matrix / heatmap

num = eda[['SeriousDlqin2yrs','RevolvingUtilizationOfUnsecuredLines','Age','NumberOfTime30-59DaysPastDueNotWorse','DebtRatio','MonthlyIncome',

for ax,m in zip(axes, ['pearson','spearman']):

    sns.heatmap(cm, annot=True, fmt='.2f', cmap='coolwarm', center=0, vmin=-1, vmax=1, mask=np.triu(np.ones_like(cm,bool),1), ax=ax, cbar=False, annot_kws={'size':8})
    ax.set_title(f'{m.title()} correlation (sentinel codes masked)')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print('Spearman correlation with target:'); display(num.corr(method='spearman')[TARGET].drop(TARGET).sort_values(key=abs, ascending=False).round(3).to_frame('spearman'))

Key insights:

  • Rank (Spearman) correlation is the trustworthy one here because the variables are skewed with outliers; Pearson is ≈0 for utilisation, income and DebtRatio (outliers swamp the signal) even though binned plots show clear effects. Strongest Spearman links with the target: # 90-day late (0.34), 60-89 late (0.27), 30-59 late (0.25), utilisation (0.24) and age (−0.12).
  • The three past-due counters are only moderately inter-correlated (≈0.2–0.3 once the 96/98 codes are masked; with the codes left in, they would look almost perfectly correlated – another artefact of the sentinel problem). Each still carries separate signal, but a combined “total late events” feature is worth testing. DebtRatio, NumberRealEstate and OpenCredit have almost no monotonic relation with the target.

3. Data Cleaning & Preparation

All steps are applied to a copy (df); the original raw frame stays untouched so the before/after can be compared. Each step is investigated first, then changed.

Order of operations: standardise categories → fix impossible values → handle sentinels → create flags → impute → cap outliers → fix dtypes.

3.1 Standardise categorical values (Gender)

df = raw.copy()
print('Before:', df.Gender.value_counts(dropna=False).to_dict())
df['Gender'] = df.Gender.astype('string').str.strip().str.lower().map({'m':'Male','f':'Female','male':'Male','female':'Female'})
print('After :', df.Gender.value_counts(dropna=False).to_dict())
print(f'Gender missing: {df.Gender.isna().mean()*100:.2f}%')
Before: {nan: 149693, 'm': 223, 'f': 84}
After : {nan: 149693, 'Male': 223, 'Female': 84}
Gender missing: 99.80%

Labels were lower-case single letters; they are now standardised to Male / Female. Decision: drop Gender from the cleaned modelling table – 99.8 % missing and only present for one slice of Ids, so any imputation would be fabricating data; additionally gender is a protected attribute in credit scoring. (Standardised labels are kept in the code above for transparency.)

df = df.drop(columns='Gender')
print('Gender dropped ->', df.shape)
Gender dropped -> (150000, 12)

3.2 Impossible values: Age

n0 = len(df)
bad = df[df.Age < 18]; print('Removing', len(bad), 'row(s) with Age < 18 (Id:', bad.Id.tolist(), ')')
df = df[df.Age >= 18].copy()
print('Rows', n0, '->', len(df))
Removing 1 row(s) with Age < 18 (Id: [65696] )
Rows 150000 -> 149999

Decision: remove the single Age = 0 record. It is impossible for a credit holder, it cannot be corrected (true age unknown), and dropping 1 row out of 150,000 costs nothing. Ages up to 109 are retained (rare but plausible).

3.3 Special codes 96 / 98 in the past-due counters

df['LateCodeFlag'] = (df[LATE]>=96).any(axis=1).astype(int)
print('Rows flagged:', df.LateCodeFlag.sum(), '| default rate among flagged:', round(df.loc[df.LateCodeFlag==1,TARGET].mean(),3))
df.loc[df.LateCodeFlag==1, LATE] = np.nan                    # codes are not real counts
print('Medians used for imputation:', df[LATE].median().to_dict())
df[LATE] = df[LATE].fillna(df[LATE].median())
print('Max after fix:', df[LATE].max().to_dict())
Rows flagged: 269 | default rate among flagged: 0.546
Medians used for imputation: {'NumberOfTime30-59DaysPastDueNotWorse': 0.0, 'NumberOfTime60-89DaysPastDueNotWorse': 0.0, 'NumberOfTimes90DaysLate': 0.0}
Max after fix: {'NumberOfTime30-59DaysPastDueNotWorse': 13.0, 'NumberOfTime60-89DaysPastDueNotWorse': 11.0, 'NumberOfTimes90DaysLate': 17.0}

Decision: the 96/98 values are placeholder codes, not counts, so they are set to NaN and imputed with the median (0). Because these rows have a 54.6 % default rate, deleting them would throw away signal – instead the binary flag LateCodeFlag preserves the information that “this borrower had a special/unknown late-payment code”. Leaving 98 in place would have been the worst option (it would dominate any linear model and scaler).

3.4 Missing & zero income, and the DebtRatio problem

df['IncomeUnknown'] = (df.MonthlyIncome.isna() | (df.MonthlyIncome==0)).astype(int)
print('IncomeUnknown = 1 :', df.IncomeUnknown.sum(), f'({df.IncomeUnknown.mean()*100:.1f}%)  | default rate', round(df.loc[df.IncomeUnknown==1,TARGET].mean(),4), 'vs', round(df.loc[df.IncomeUnknown==0,TARGET].mean(),4))
ok = df.IncomeUnknown==0
print('\nDebtRatio – income known  :', df.loc[ok,'DebtRatio'].quantile([.5,.9,.99]).round(3).to_dict())
print('DebtRatio – income unknown:', df.loc[~ok,'DebtRatio'].quantile([.5,.9,.99]).round(1).to_dict())
IncomeUnknown = 1 : 31365 (20.9%)  | default rate 0.0553 vs 0.0699

DebtRatio – income known  : {0.5: 0.292, 0.9: 0.725, 0.99: 2.994}
DebtRatio – income unknown: {0.5: 1144.0, 0.9: 3773.2, 0.99: 8174.1}

Decision (income): treat NaN and 0 as unknown income (zeros come with the same dollar-style DebtRatio as missing values, so they are almost certainly “not recorded”). Create flag IncomeUnknown, then impute income with the median of the borrower’s age band (income is highly skewed so the mean would be inflated by the 3 M outlier; age band captures part of the life-cycle income pattern). Imputing with a constant/mean or deleting 20 % of the data would both be worse: deleting would remove ~30 k borrowers and bias the sample; the flag lets the model still use the missingness signal.

Decision (DebtRatio): for IncomeUnknown = 1 rows, DebtRatio is a dollar amount and cannot be converted to a ratio (the denominator is unknown). Where it is > 1 it is set to NaN and imputed with the median DebtRatio of valid rows; the flag marks these rows. Rows with known income keep their (genuine) ratios, including legitimately large ones in 1–2.

# --- income imputation: median of age band computed on KNOWN incomes only
band = pd.cut(df.Age,[0,25,35,45,55,65,75,120],labels=False)
known = df.MonthlyIncome.where(df.IncomeUnknown==0)
med_by_band = known.groupby(band).median(); print('Median income by age band:', med_by_band.round(0).to_dict())
df['MonthlyIncome'] = known.fillna(band.map(med_by_band))

# --- DebtRatio: dollar-valued entries for unknown-income rows -> NaN -> median of valid ratios
bad_dr = (df.IncomeUnknown==1) & (df.DebtRatio>1)
print('DebtRatio entries treated as unreliable:', bad_dr.sum())
valid_med = df.loc[df.IncomeUnknown==0,'DebtRatio'].median()
df.loc[bad_dr,'DebtRatio'] = np.nan
df['DebtRatio'] = df.DebtRatio.fillna(valid_med)
print('Median valid DebtRatio used:', round(valid_med,4))
print('Missing income left:', df.MonthlyIncome.isna().sum())
Median income by age band: {0: 1727.0, 1: 3948.0, 2: 5700.0, 3: 6333.0, 4: 6233.0, 5: 5200.0, 6: 4276.0}
DebtRatio entries treated as unreliable: 29425
Median valid DebtRatio used: 0.2924
Missing income left: 0

3.5 Missing NumberOfDependents

print('Dependents missing:', df.NumberOfDependents.isna().sum(), '| of which IncomeUnknown:', int(df.loc[df.NumberOfDependents.isna(),'IncomeUnknown'].sum()))
print('Mode / median:', df.NumberOfDependents.mode()[0], df.NumberOfDependents.median())
df['NumberOfDependents'] = df.NumberOfDependents.fillna(df.NumberOfDependents.mode()[0])
print('Missing after:', df.NumberOfDependents.isna().sum())
Dependents missing: 3924 | of which IncomeUnknown: 3924
Mode / median: 0.0 0.0
Missing after: 0

Decision: impute with the mode/median = 0 (≈59 % of borrowers have 0 dependents; the variable is a discrete count so the mean 0.76 would give an impossible fractional value). Only 2.6 % are affected, they are all already inside the IncomeUnknown group, so no extra flag is needed.

3.6 Outliers — investigate, then cap

cap_info = {}
u = df.RevolvingUtilizationOfUnsecuredLines
print('Utilisation: >1 =', (u>1).sum(), '| >2 =', (u>2).sum(), '| >10 =', (u>10).sum(), '| default rate of >2 rows:', round(df.loc[u>2,TARGET].mean(),3))
print('Income (after imputation) q99/q99.5/q99.9:', df.MonthlyIncome.quantile([.99,.995,.999]).round(0).to_dict())
print('DebtRatio q99/q99.9:', df.DebtRatio.quantile([.99,.999]).round(2).to_dict())
print('OpenCredit q99.9:', df.NumberOfOpenCreditLinesAndLoans.quantile(.999), '| RealEstate q99.9:', df.NumberRealEstateLoansOrLines.quantile(.999))
Utilisation: >1 = 3321 | >2 = 371 | >10 = 241 | default rate of >2 rows: 0.146
Income (after imputation) q99/q99.5/q99.9: {0.99: 23000.0, 0.995: 31250.0, 0.999: 72759.0}
DebtRatio q99/q99.9: {0.99: 2.33, 0.999: 1305.0}
OpenCredit q99.9: 34.0 | RealEstate q99.9: 9.0

# Winsorise (cap) – keep every row, just limit the leverage of extreme values
df['UtilOver1'] = (df.RevolvingUtilizationOfUnsecuredLines>1).astype(int)       # keep the 'over-limit' information
caps = {
 'RevolvingUtilizationOfUnsecuredLines': 2.0,                                   # >2x limit is implausible; domain-based cap
 'MonthlyIncome': df.MonthlyIncome.quantile(.995),                              # 99.5th percentile
 'DebtRatio': df.loc[df.IncomeUnknown==0,'DebtRatio'].quantile(.99),            # 99th pct of genuine ratios
 'NumberOfOpenCreditLinesAndLoans': df.NumberOfOpenCreditLinesAndLoans.quantile(.999),
 'NumberRealEstateLoansOrLines': df.NumberRealEstateLoansOrLines.quantile(.999),
}
rows=[]
for c,cap in caps.items():
    n=(df[c]>cap).sum(); df[c]=df[c].clip(upper=cap); rows.append({'variable':c,'cap':round(cap,3),'rows capped':n})
display(pd.DataFrame(rows))
variable cap rows capped
0 RevolvingUtilizationOfUnsecuredLines 2.0000 371
1 MonthlyIncome 31,250.0000 740
2 DebtRatio 2.9940 1187
3 NumberOfOpenCreditLinesAndLoans 34.0000 146
4 NumberRealEstateLoansOrLines 9.0000 131

Decision: cap (winsorise) rather than remove or keep as-is.

  • Not removing: the affected rows are real borrowers with otherwise valid information; removal would also shed a disproportionate number of defaulters (e.g. utilisation 1–2× has a 40 % default rate).
  • Not keeping as-is: values like utilisation = 50,708 or income = 3 M carry no extra meaning beyond “very high”, and would dominate scaling and linear/distance-based models.
  • Caps: utilisation at 2 (domain logic), income at the 99.5th percentile, DebtRatio at the 99th percentile of genuine ratios, and the two count variables at the 99.9th percentile. An UtilOver1 flag preserves the “over the limit” signal. Past-due counters (max 17 after fixing the codes) are real and kept unchanged.

3.7 Correct data types

int_cols = ['NumberOfDependents']+LATE+['NumberOfOpenCreditLinesAndLoans','NumberRealEstateLoansOrLines']

for c in ['SeriousDlqin2yrs','LateCodeFlag','IncomeUnknown','UtilOver1']: df[c]=df[c].astype('int8')
df['Age']=df.Age.astype('int16')
df['Id']=df.Id.astype('int32')
df = df.set_index('Id')            # identifier, not a feature
df = df[[TARGET]+[c for c in df.columns if c!=TARGET]]
df.dtypes.to_frame('dtype')

Key insight: After cleaning, no value is missing, the ranges are plausible (utilisation ≤ 2, DebtRatio ≤ 3, income ≤ 31,250) and the skewness of the three problem variables drops from ≈95–114 to ≈1–4, while only 1 of 150,000 rows was removed and the target distribution is unchanged (6.68 %).

4. Final Findings

4.1 Most important data-quality issues

  • Special codes (96/98) in all three past-due counters (269 rows, 54.6 % default) – would massively distort any model if read as counts.
  • DebtRatio is not a ratio for borrowers with missing/zero income – values median ≈1,000 vs 0.29; ≈84 % of rows with ratio > 1 are of this type, making the raw feature misleading.
  • Missing and zero MonthlyIncome (≈ 20 % missing + 1,634 zeros), informative (different default rate) and co-occurring with missing dependents.
  • Gender is 99.8 % empty and non-random (only in the first ≈16k Ids) → unusable.
  • Impossible / extreme values: Age = 0, utilisation up to 50,708, income up to ≈3 M; plus a heavily imbalanced target (6.68 %).

4.2 Meaningful EDA insights

  • Only 6.68 % defaulted (≈14 : 1 imbalance) – accuracy is a misleading metric.
  • Past-due history is the strongest predictor: one 90-day delinquency raises default from ≈4.6 % to ≈34 %; three or more → ≈58–67 %.
  • Credit utilisation is a strong, monotonic driver: ≈2 % default below 25 % utilisation vs ≈18 % at 75–100 % and ≈40 % when over the limit.
  • Younger borrowers are riskier: ≈11 % default under 36 vs ≈2 % over 65 (mean age 45.9 vs 52.8).
  • Higher income → lower risk (≈8–10 % in the bottom deciles vs ≈4.5 % in the top), but with diminishing effect; missing income has its own (lower, 5.6 %) rate.
  • Raw DebtRatio looks uninformative (even decreasing at high values) only because of the income problem; with valid income, risk rises from ≈6 % to ≈14 % for ratios 1–2.
  • Rank correlation beats Pearson here: Spearman picks up the past-due counters (0.25–0.34), utilisation (0.24) and age (−0.12), whereas Pearson is ≈0 for skewed variables; the three past-due counters overlap only moderately (≈0.2–0.3) and the 96/98 codes would have faked a near-perfect correlation.

4.3 Main cleaning / preparation decisions

ProblemDecisionWhy
GenderStandardised, then dropped99.8 % missing, non-random, sensitive attribute
Age = 0Row removed (1 row)Impossible, not recoverable, negligible loss
96/98 codes→ NaN, median-imputed, LateCodeFlagPlaceholder codes; flag preserves the strong signal
Missing/zero incomeIncomeUnknown flag + age-band medianSkew-robust, keeps 20 % of the data, keeps missingness signal
DebtRatio (unknown income)Dollar-valued entries → NaN → median of valid ratiosNot a real ratio; denominator unknown
Missing dependentsMode (0)Discrete count; mean gives impossible fractions
OutliersCapped (util 2; income p99.5; DebtRatio p99; counts p99.9) + UtilOver1Keeps all rows/defaulters, limits leverage
Duplicates0 exact; 608 feature-twins investigated and keptDistinct Ids, thin-file profiles – legitimately identical
TypesCounts → int, flags → int8, Id → indexCorrect semantics, memory

Shape: 150,000 × 13 → 149,999 × 14 (−1 row, −Gender, +3 flags: LateCodeFlag, IncomeUnknown, UtilOver1; Id is the index, so the saved CSV has 15 columns including Id).

4.4 Things to check before using this dataset for ML

  • Class imbalance (6.68 %) – use stratified train/test split & cross-validation, class weights or resampling, and evaluate with AUC / PR-AUC / recall, not accuracy.
  • Fit imputers/caps on the training set only – the medians and percentile caps here were computed on the full data for exploration; in a pipeline they must be learnt on train and applied to validation/test to avoid data leakage.
  • Confirm the meaning of 96/98 codes and zero-income and the DebtRatio definition with the data owner; also confirm whether Gender was intentionally collected for a subset (and whether it should be used at all – fairness/regulatory review).
  • Feature engineering & scaling: the three past-due counters overlap moderately (test a combined “total late events” feature) and check VIF; skewed variables benefit from log/robust transforms for linear or distance-based models.
  • Target definition / time-window and representativeness: check that all features are measured before the 2-year outcome window (no leakage), that there is no temporal drift, and that the 20 % income-unknown segment is represented in production data the same way.
